INHERITANCE DISQUALIFICATION FOR ELDER OR DEPENDENT ADULT ABUSE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Smith

PURPOSE OF THIS INHERITANCE DISQUALIFICATION FOR ELDER OR DEPENDENT ADULT ABUSE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California Probate Code § 259 — part of Probate Code Part 7, “Effect of Homicide or Abuse of an Elder or Dependent Adult” (Prob. Code §§ 250–259) — a statute that can disqualify a person from inheriting from, or serving as a fiduciary for, John Smith, an elder or dependent adult decedent, based on specific findings or a criminal conviction concerning that person's abuse of John Smith during John Smith's lifetime. It states general facts about how § 259 works: the conditions that can trigger disqualification, the “deemed to have predeceased” mechanism the statute uses to describe the consequence, and the definitions § 259 cross-references. It is not a finding, determination, accusation, or admission that any specific person abused John Smith, and it does not identify, name, or make any claim about any individual. This Information Sheet is distinct from two other, related documents in this corpus. It is not the corpus's Slayer Statute — Disqualification from Inheriting Information Sheet, which describes Prob. Code §§ 250–254, the separate statutory scheme disqualifying a person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent; § 259 instead addresses abuse of a decedent who was an elder or dependent adult during that person's lifetime, applies its own distinct evidentiary requirements, and does not require that the abuse caused the decedent's death. It is also not the corpus's Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet, which describes the civil damages remedies that Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 15657.5 and 15657.7 make available to, or on behalf of, an elder or dependent adult during that person's life; § 259 instead operates after the elder or dependent adult's death, as part of distributing that person's own estate, and its consequence is disqualification from inheriting or serving as a fiduciary rather than a money-damages award. This Information Sheet is prepared by Jane Doe in connection with the estate of John Smith.

THE CIVIL PATH: FOUR FINDINGS REQUIRED TO DISQUALIFY UNDER §259(A)
Probate Code § 259(a) allows a person to be deemed to have predeceased the decedent — with the consequence described in § 259(c) — only where all four of the following are found. First, it must be proven by clear and convincing evidence, a higher standard than the ordinary civil preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, that the person is liable for physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse of the decedent, who was an elder or dependent adult. Second, the person must be found to have acted in bad faith. Third, the person must be found to have been reckless, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious in committing the abuse. Fourth, the decedent must be found to have been substantially unable to manage their financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence at the time the abuse occurred and thereafter until the decedent's death. All four findings are required for this civil path; § 259(a) does not disqualify a person based on a liability finding alone, and its list of conduct that can support the liability finding — physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse — does not include false imprisonment, which enters § 259 only through the separate criminal-conviction path in § 259(b). Whether John Smith met the statutory definition of an elder or dependent adult, and whether these four findings have been made concerning John Smith's estate, are facts this Information Sheet does not determine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Any person shall be deemed to have predeceased a decedent to the extent provided in subdivision (c) where all of the following apply: (1) It has been proven by clear and convincing evidence that the person is liable for physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse of the decedent, who was an elder or dependent adult. (2) The person is found to have acted in bad faith. (3) The person has been found to have been reckless, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious in the commission of any of these acts upon the decedent. (4) The decedent, at the time those acts occurred and thereafter until the time of his or her death, has been found to have been substantially unable to manage his or her financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 259(a), California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the four findings required for the civil path (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=259.)
  Known gap: This citation covers all of Prob. Code § 259(a), including its four numbered requirements, (a)(1)-(4), as a single subdivision of one statutory section; it has not been checked against any other code section. This clause does not cover the criminal-conviction path in § 259(b), the disqualification's effect and its regained-capacity limit in § 259(c), or the cross-referenced definitions in § 259(d) (each addressed by a separate clause in this document). It also does not address the procedure by which a court makes these findings — in what proceeding, on whose petition, at what point in estate administration — because § 259 itself does not specify that procedure and this research did not independently investigate it.

THE CRIMINAL-CONVICTION PATH: §259(B) AND THE PENAL CODE OFFENSES IT CROSS-REFERENCES
Probate Code § 259(b) provides a second, independent path to being deemed to have predeceased the decedent: a person convicted of a violation of Penal Code § 236 — California's general false imprisonment offense, defined as “the unlawful violation of the personal liberty of another” — or of any offense described in Penal Code § 368 is deemed to have predeceased the decedent, without the separate clear-and-convincing findings that § 259(a)'s civil path requires. Penal Code § 368, part of the Penal Code chapter titled “Crimes Against Elders, Dependent Adults, and Persons with Disabilities,” describes a range of offenses against a person the defendant knows or reasonably should know is an elder or dependent adult, including, under § 368(b)(1), willfully causing or permitting an elder or dependent adult to suffer unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering, or to be injured or endangered, under circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death; under § 368(d), theft, embezzlement, forgery, fraud, or identity theft against an elder's or dependent adult's property or personal identifying information by a person who is not the victim's caretaker; and, under § 368(f), false imprisonment of an elder or dependent adult specifically by the use of violence, menace, fraud, or deceit — the § 368 provision that corresponds to § 259(d)(3)'s cross-referenced definition of “false imprisonment,” as the definitions clause of this Information Sheet describes. Whether John Smith's estate involves a conviction of this kind, and if so under which subdivision of § 236 or § 368, is a fact this Information Sheet does not determine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) Any person shall be deemed to have predeceased a decedent to the extent provided in subdivision (c) if that person has been convicted of a violation of Section 236 of the Penal Code or any offense described in Section 368 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 259(b), California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the criminal-conviction path (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=259.)
  "False imprisonment is the unlawful violation of the personal liberty of another."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 236, California Penal Code, general false imprisonment offense (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=236.)
  "(b) (1) A person who knows or reasonably should know that a person is an elder or dependent adult and who, under circumstances or conditions likely to produce great bodily harm or death, willfully causes or permits any elder or dependent adult to suffer, or inflicts thereon unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering, or having the care or custody of any elder or dependent adult, willfully causes or permits the person or health of the elder or dependent adult to be injured, or willfully causes or permits the elder or dependent adult to be placed in a situation in which their person or health is endangered, is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by a fine not to exceed six thousand dollars ($6,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment, or by imprisonment in the state prison for two, three, or four years."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 368(b)(1), California Penal Code, elder/dependent adult abuse — physical pain, suffering, injury, or endangerment offense (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=368.)
  "(d) A person who is not a caretaker who violates any provision of law proscribing theft, embezzlement, forgery, or fraud, or who violates Section 530.5 proscribing identity theft, with respect to the property or personal identifying information of an elder or a dependent adult, and who knows or reasonably should know that the victim is an elder or a dependent adult, is punishable as follows:"
  — Cal. Penal Code § 368(d), California Penal Code, elder/dependent adult abuse — theft, embezzlement, forgery, fraud, or identity theft offense (non-caretaker) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=368.)
  "(f) A person who commits the false imprisonment of an elder or a dependent adult by the use of violence, menace, fraud, or deceit is punishable by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 for two, three, or four years."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 368(f), California Penal Code, elder/dependent adult abuse — false imprisonment by violence, menace, fraud, or deceit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=368.)
  Known gap: Prob. Code § 259(b), Penal Code § 236, and Penal Code § 368 are independent statutory sections in different codes, not subdivisions of one section; § 259(b) is the Probate Code provision that cross-references the other two. Penal Code § 368 has additional subdivisions this clause does not quote or independently verify beyond (b)(1), (d), and (f): among them § 368(a) (a legislative-findings preamble), § 368(c) (a misdemeanor version of the § 368(b)(1) conduct), § 368(e) (the caretaker-specific version of the § 368(d) theft offense), § 368(g)-(i) (definitions of ‘elder,’ ‘dependent adult,’ and ‘caretaker’ for purposes of § 368 itself, which are not necessarily identical to the Welfare and Institutions Code definitions the rest of this document and the corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet use), and § 368(j)-(l) (sentencing and other procedural provisions). This clause does not address how ‘any offense described in Section 368’ applies to a conviction resting on a subdivision not summarized here.

THE PREDECEASE MECHANISM: WHAT DISQUALIFICATION BARS, AND THE REGAINED-CAPACITY LIMIT
Probate Code § 259(c) states the consequence for a person found liable under § 259(a) or convicted under § 259(b). That person shall not receive any property, damages, or costs awarded to the decedent's estate in the action establishing the abuse — whether the person's entitlement would otherwise arise under a will, a trust, or the laws of intestacy — and shall not serve as a fiduciary, as Prob. Code § 39 defines that term, if the instrument nominating or appointing the person was executed while the decedent was substantially unable to manage their financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. Unlike the general slayer statute's predecease mechanism in Prob. Code § 250(b), § 259(c) does not itself say the disqualified person is treated “as if” they had predeceased the decedent; instead, § 259(a) and § 259(b) each independently state that the disqualified person “shall be deemed to have predeceased” the decedent “to the extent provided in subdivision (c),” and § 259(c) is where that extent is defined — the bar on receiving estate property, damages, or costs, and the bar on serving as a nominated fiduciary, described above. Section 259(c) also states a limit: the section does not apply to a decedent who, at any time after the abusive act or acts, was substantially able to manage their financial resources and resist fraud or undue influence, within the meaning of Prob. Code § 1801(b) and Civil Code § 39(b) — meaning a decedent's later, sufficiently established regained capacity can take the decedent's estate outside § 259's disqualification rule entirely, even where the § 259(a) findings or a § 259(b) conviction would otherwise apply. Whether that limit applies to John Smith's estate is a fact this Information Sheet does not determine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) Any person found liable under subdivision (a) or convicted under subdivision (b) shall not (1) receive any property, damages, or costs that are awarded to the decedent’s estate in an action described in subdivision (a) or (b), whether that person’s entitlement is under a will, a trust, or the laws of intestacy; or (2) serve as a fiduciary as defined in Section 39, if the instrument nominating or appointing that person was executed during the period when the decedent was substantially unable to manage his or her financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. This section shall not apply to a decedent who, at any time following the act or acts described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), or the act or acts described in subdivision (b), was substantially able to manage his or her financial resources and to resist fraud or undue influence within the meaning of subdivision (b) of Section 1801 of the Probate Code and subdivision (b) of Section 39 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 259(c), California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the predecease consequence and the regained-capacity limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=259.)
  Known gap: This citation covers all of Prob. Code § 259(c) as a single subdivision. Section 259(c)'s own text cross-references Prob. Code § 39 (defining ‘fiduciary’), Prob. Code § 1801(b), and Civil Code § 39(b) (both bearing on the capacity standard used for the regained-capacity limit); this research fetched and verified Prob. Code § 259 itself but did not independently fetch or verify the text of Prob. Code § 39, Prob. Code § 1801(b), or Civil Code § 39(b), so this clause's description of those three cross-referenced provisions is limited to how § 259(c) itself characterizes them, not to their full, independently verified text. This clause does not restate the § 259(a) findings or the § 259(b) conviction path themselves (covered by earlier clauses).

CROSS-REFERENCED DEFINITIONS UNDER §259(D)
Probate Code § 259(d) does not define its four key terms itself; it cross-references other code sections. “Physical abuse” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.63, which lists categories including assault, battery, assault with a deadly weapon or force likely to produce great bodily injury, unreasonable physical constraint, and prolonged or continual deprivation of food or water, as well as (in subdivisions this clause does not separately quote) several forms of sexual assault and use of a physical or chemical restraint or psychotropic medication for punishment, beyond a physician's ordered period, or for an unauthorized purpose. “Neglect” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.57(a) as, in relevant part, the negligent failure of a person having care or custody of an elder or dependent adult — or of an elder or dependent adult personally — to exercise the degree of care a reasonable person in a like position would exercise; § 15610.57(b), not separately quoted here, lists non-exclusive examples including failure to assist with personal hygiene, food, clothing, or shelter, failure to provide needed medical care, failure to protect from health and safety hazards, failure to prevent malnutrition or dehydration, and substantial inability or failure to manage one's own finances. “False imprisonment” is defined by cross-reference to Penal Code § 368 rather than to the Penal Code's general false imprisonment offense in § 236, because — as the criminal-conviction-path clause of this Information Sheet describes — § 368(f) contains an elder- and dependent-adult-specific false imprisonment offense, and it is that specific offense to which § 259(d)(3) points. “Financial abuse” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.30, the same definition described in the corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet, which this Information Sheet does not separately restate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(d) For purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply: (1) “Physical abuse” as defined in Section 15610.63 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (2) “Neglect” as defined in Section 15610.57 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (3) “False imprisonment” as defined in Section 368 of the Penal Code. (4) “Financial abuse” as defined in Section 15610.30 of the Welfare and Institutions Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 259(d), California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — cross-referenced definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=259.)
  "“Physical abuse” means any of the following: (a) Assault, as defined in Section 240 of the Penal Code. (b) Battery, as defined in Section 242 of the Penal Code. (c) Assault with a deadly weapon or force likely to produce great bodily injury, as defined in Section 245 of the Penal Code. (d) Unreasonable physical constraint, or prolonged or continual deprivation of food or water."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.63(a)-(d), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.63, “physical abuse” (chapeau and subdivisions (a)-(d)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.63.)
  "(a) “Neglect” means either of the following: (1) The negligent failure of any person having the care or custody of an elder or a dependent adult to exercise that degree of care that a reasonable person in a like position would exercise. (2) The negligent failure of an elder or dependent adult to exercise that degree of self care that a reasonable person in a like position would exercise."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.57(a), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.57(a), “neglect” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.57.)
  Known gap: The Prob. Code § 259(d) citation covers all four numbered definitions, (d)(1)-(4), as a single subdivision. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.63 and § 15610.57 are independent sections, not subdivisions of § 259 or of each other. The § 15610.63 citation quotes only its chapeau and subdivisions (a)-(d) (assault, battery, assault with a deadly weapon, and unreasonable restraint or food/water deprivation); it does not quote § 15610.63(e) (a list of eight sexual-assault offenses defined by further cross-reference to the Penal Code) or § 15610.63(f) (the restraint-or-psychotropic-medication list), though the body above summarizes both without quoting them verbatim. The § 15610.57 citation quotes only its subdivision (a) (the two-prong negligent-failure definition); it does not quote § 15610.57(b) (the seven-item non-exclusive illustrative list) or § 15610.57(c) (treating homelessness as neglect under specified conditions), though the body summarizes several (b) items without quoting them verbatim. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30 (financial abuse), because that section is already fetched, verified, and quoted in this corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet (clause elderabuse_financial_abuse_definition); this clause points to that existing coverage rather than duplicating it.

SEVERANCE TO A SEPARATE CIVIL ACTION
Probate Code § 259(e) states that nothing in § 259 is to be construed to prohibit the severance and transfer of an action or proceeding to a separate civil action under Prob. Code § 801. Section 801 is a general probate-jurisdiction provision, not specific to § 259: it allows the court, on its own motion or a party's motion, to order that an action or proceeding not specifically provided for in the Probate Code be determined in a separate civil action, and, once the appropriate filing fees are paid, to order the severed action or proceeding transferred to that separate civil action. Section 259(e) thus confirms that a § 259 disqualification dispute is not required to be resolved entirely within the probate proceeding itself; § 801's general severance-and-transfer mechanism remains available for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(e) Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit the severance and transfer of an action or proceeding to a separate civil action pursuant to Section 801."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 259(e), California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — severance to a separate civil action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=259.)
  "The court, on its own motion or on the motion of any interested party, may order that an action or proceeding not specifically provided in this code be determined in a separate civil action. Upon the payment of the appropriate filing fees, the court may order transfer of the severed action or proceeding to the separate civil action."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 801, California Probate Code, general severance and transfer to a separate civil action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=801.)
  Known gap: Prob. Code § 259(e) and Prob. Code § 801 are independent sections, though § 259(e) is the specific provision confirming § 801 applies to a § 259 dispute. Section 801 is a general Probate Code jurisdiction provision (Division 2, Part 16) that applies well beyond § 259; this clause describes only its severance-and-transfer mechanism as § 259(e) invokes it, not the whole of Part 16's jurisdictional scheme, and does not address what other Probate Code provisions besides § 259 rely on § 801.

CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURE — INHERITANCE DISQUALIFICATION FOR ELDER OR DEPENDENT ADULT ABUSE INFORMATION SHEET
I, Jane Doe, certify that I have read this Information Sheet describing Probate Code § 259 in connection with the estate of John Smith, that it states generally applicable California law rather than a conclusion about any actual person's conduct toward John Smith, and that whether the findings § 259(a) requires have been made, whether a conviction described in § 259(b) has occurred, and whether § 259(c)'s regained-capacity limit applies are all determinations for a court in the estate proceeding — not something this Information Sheet determines, and not something it advises Jane Doe on.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jane Doe: _________________________

Printed name: _________________________

Section 259(c) also states a limit: the section does not apply to a decedent who, at any time after the abusive act or acts, was substantially able to manage their financial resources and resist fraud or undue influence, within the meaning of Prob. Code § 1801(b) and Civil Code § 39(b) — meaning a decedent's later, sufficiently established regained capacity can take the decedent's estate outside § 259's disqualification rule entirely, even where the § 259(a) findings or a § 259(b) conviction would otherwise apply. Whether that limit applies to John Smith's estate is a fact this Information Sheet does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 259(e) states that nothing in § 259 is to be construed to prohibit the severance and transfer of an action or proceeding to a separate civil action under Prob. Code § 801. Section 801 is a general probate-jurisdiction provision, not specific to § 259: it allows the court, on its own motion or a party's motion, to order that an action or proceeding not specifically provided for in the Probate Code be determined in a separate civil action, and, once the appropriate filing fees are paid, to order the severed action or proceeding transferred to that separate civil action. Section 259(e) thus confirms that a § 259 disqualification dispute is not required to be resolved entirely within the probate proceeding itself; § 801's general severance-and-transfer mechanism remains available for it.
